lines.note: Tomodachi denotes companions or comrades; the Portuguese pairs travelling or shipboard companions with the broader companheiros.

Tomodochi is the poetic form referred to Tomodachi, with Idem retaining the same meaning. The scan has a comma after the explanatory i. The isolated P. keeps the baseline roman setting; its slight slant is not decisive against neighbouring roman types.
Tomodori and the alternative Tomotori name a rower stationed near the rudder; re- begins rema on the following line.
Completes rema: the rower rows beside the rudder. This short continuation belongs to the nautical entry, before the homonymous bird entry.

runs.text: Paßaros de hũa meſma eſpecie que

lines.note: Tomodori here denotes birds of the same species; the description continues with their flying together. The homonymous entry is distinct from the preceding rower.
The birds fly together, completing the explanation of Tomodori. The printed vão and voando retain the source’s spelling and tilde.

runs.text: Os, ou aquelles, peßoa, ou gente.

lines.note: Tomogara refers to those people or that company, matching aquelles, peßoa, and gente. The Portuguese list is retained without imposing a single modern equivalent.

runs.text: Coxas das pernas da bãda de fora.

lines.note: Tomomo is glossed as the outer sides of the thighs, in contrast to Vchimomo below. The printed short headword is retained rather than expanded to a modern expected compound.
Vchimomo gives the contrasting inner thighs. As refers back to coxas, so this is an interior-versus-exterior contrast within the anatomical explanation.
Tômon is explained as Figaxino mon, an eastward gate; the Portuguese specifies a street or outer gate facing toward the east. The scan shows the circumflex.
Oriente completes the eastward direction of the gate. The initial is the round capital O, not the OCR Griente.
Tomonai, with its supplied principal parts, means accompanying someone. The visibly separated A companhar is preserved as printed instead of joined to modern acompanhar.

runs.text: Fitoua tada vareni fitoxij fitouo to-

lines.note: The example says that a person should accompany someone equal to himself. Fitoua and vareni remain joined exactly as printed; to- continues into the verb below.

Monauǒ completes the divided verb in the recommendation to associate with one’s equals. Fab. supplies the citation label; Os homens ande begins the Portuguese explanation, retaining the printed contraction.

runs.text: andar, ou tratar com os de ſua laya.

lines.note: Completes the advice: people should go about or associate with those of their own sort. Laya expresses kind or class in this explanation.
Tomoni means with, in company, or together. The rounded o in Tomoni and the initial C of Com correct the OCR Tamoni and Cem.
Tanto que adds the temporal connective sense, as soon as; it continues the range of uses of Tomoni rather than beginning another entry.
Tomoni motte is referred back to the same meanings by Idem. The Japanese expression remains roman and the gloss italic.

runs.text: Remo, ou remeiro do cabo, ou mais

lines.note: Tomoro means the stern oar or its rower. The following line locates it nearest the rudder, clarifying the nautical sense.
Completes the position of Tomoro: the oar or oarsman closest to the rudder. It is a continuation of the preceding paired definition.
Tomosureba is equated with yayamosureba, describing something frequent or liable to recur. The visible e in the second sureba corrects OCR Yayamoſuroba.
Ou frequentemente completes the adverbial gloss: frequently, or at every turn. This belongs to the conditional expression above.

Tǒmot is equated with karamono, an object from China. The worn, compact central m is read provisionally; it and the visible r of Caramono correct the malformed OCR; the final bare t is the printed checked ending. The supplied NINJAL Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, record 260c13, corroborates the lexical identification after visual reading (NINJAL; Hideyuki Ohshima, with Taichi Aida; version 202510; CC BY 4.0; https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html). The scan controls this copy’s exact form.

runs.text: Cadeira onde ſe aßenta o piloto,

lines.note: Tomoyacata is the seat where the pilot sits. The next line gives the Japanese occupational name and locates the seat on a vessel.

runs.text: ou Xendǒ na embarcação, ou nauio.

lines.note: The pilot is also called Xendǒ, a Japanese occupational name embedded within the Portuguese explanation of the vessel. Enlargement shows the caron over o and italic type throughout; the OCR split after X was spurious.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de pintura como ſe faz

lines.note: Tomoye names a decorative design. The Portuguese introduces its occurrence on roof tiles and clothing rather than defining an abstract geometric figure.

runs.text: nas pontas das telhas, ou tambem nos veſtidos,

lines.note: The design occurs on the ends of roof tiles and also on clothing. This continues the description of Tomoye and its practical locations.
It also appears elsewhere as a device or emblem; divisa supplies that functional sense. The list closes the description begun two lines above.
Tomoyeno maru is referred to the same design by Idem, retaining the printed possessive construction and separate maru.

runs.text: Certa corda großa da popa do na-

lines.note: Tomozzuna denotes a thick stern rope or mooring line. The initial T is visible, correcting OCR romozzuna; na- begins nauio on the next line.
Nauio and amarra complete the nautical definition; Tomozzunauo toqu means loosening the stern rope. The example keeps its printed joined object particle.
The Portuguese explains casting off or unmooring the boat. Fune is a Japanese noun embedded in the Portuguese sentence; its italic setting is retained from the scan.
Tomurai here means performing funeral obsequies or pious acts for the deceased. The Portuguese commendação is divided after the nasal abbreviation cõ-.

runs.text: mendação, & obras pias por algum de funto,

lines.note: Continues the funeral sense with commendation and pious works for a deceased person. The printed de funto is kept with its spacing.
Goxeuo tomurǒ concerns performing rites for the afterlife of the deceased; Idem identifies it with the preceding funeral practice.
The noun Tomurai, alternatively toburai, denotes funeral obsequies or a funeral procession. It is distinguished from the preceding verb by its form and gloss.

runs.text: ou commendação por algum de funto.

lines.note: Completes the noun definition with commendation for a deceased person. The physical continuation and historical de funto spacing are retained.
A second Tomurai verb entry means visiting someone or inquiring after him. This is the visiting sense of the word rather than the funeral sense above.
Guntar completes perguntar: inquiring after that person. The short continuation remains a separate physical line.
Tômuxiro is a mat made of rattan or wicker. The print has the closed-o circumflex, and the Portuguese retains rota as its material name.
Tonaca is the middle of the gulf or open sea, glossed by Meo do golfão. The concise geographical definition stands as its own entry.

Ton-ai denotes absorbed attachment; the Portuguese explicitly says it is pronounced Tonnai. The colon and the letter sequence pronuncia correct the OCR punctuation and pronuteia; the embedded pronunciation is roman.

runs.text: estar entregue, ou affeiçoado a algũa couſa.

lines.note: Completes O estar: being devoted or attached to something. This explains the psychological attachment of Ton-ai rather than the pronunciation note.
Tônan combines Figaxi and minami, east and south. The two Japanese directions explain the compound; they are ordinary synonyms, not Portuguese-embedded terms for typeface tagging.

Tǒnan concerns suffering by the sword, explained as Catanano nangui. Enlargement shows the surviving downward mark, agreeing with the caron in the example below and distinguishing this entry from preceding Tônan. The supplied NINJAL index, record 260c25, corroborates the lexical distinction.
Tǒnanni vǒ illustrates encountering this sword-related misfortune. The example visibly carries a caron in Tǒnanni; the Portuguese begins the explanation of encountering it.

runs.text: este mal, ou trabalho de ſer morto à eſpada.

lines.note: Completes the misfortune as being killed by the sword. This is body text ending column 1, independent of the right-column catchword below.
Tǒ nanban pairs China with India in the Portuguese gloss. Retain the historical geographical identification rather than extending nanban to every later sense.
Tonari means a neighbour, directly translated as Vizinho. This short entry supplies the referent of Idem in the next row.

Tonariǔdo is another name for a neighbour, referred back to Tonari. Enlargement shows a marked u followed by do, rather than the OCR fido; the long-u form is retained without replacing it by modern tonaribito. The supplied NINJAL index, record 260d03, corroborates this lexical form after inspection.
Tonaye is an invocation or blessing. The following verbal entry develops the church uses of the same stem.
Tonaye, with its principal parts, means invoking or blessing something. The final al- continues into algũa on the next physical row.

Cruzno monuo tonayuru is the example for making the sign of the cross. Cruz is the Portuguese religious word incorporated in the Japanese phrase; the scan retains monuo rather than supplying an expected alternate noun.
The Portuguese first renders making the sign of the cross; the next example begins Conta nadouo, concerning beads and similar objects. Cruz corrects the OCR Craz.
Tonayuru completes the example of blessing beads. The initial t is visible and corrects OCR conayuru; pala- begins the usage explanation palavra da Igreja.
Palavra da Igreja marks this as ecclesiastical usage. Minauo tonayuru then illustrates invoking a sacred name, with the Portuguese translation beginning In-.

runs.text: uocar o nome ſanto de alguem.

lines.note: Completes inuocar: invoking someone’s holy name. This translates Minauo tonayuru and closes the sequence of blessing and invocation examples.
Tonaye qitari describes a doctrine or law coming down through time. The abbreviated principal parts remain as printed and doutri- continues below.

runs.text: na, ou ley per dedução guardandoa todos, &c.

lines.note: The doctrine or law is transmitted in succession with everyone observing it. The scan joins guardandoa, retaining its object pronoun instead of the OCR separation guardando a.
Tonayevxinai means losing a religious practice or worship over time. The embedded initial v of vxinai is the printed historical spelling, not an omitted vowel.

runs.text: veneração de Deos, ou outra couſa ſagrada por

lines.note: The lost worship concerns God or another sacred object. The Portuguese continues into the duration over successive times or generations below.
Tempos and idades complete the temporal qualification: through times and ages. It remains part of losing the cult or veneration, not a new definition.
Tonbiǒ is equated with niwakana yamai, a sudden illness. The Portuguese doença repẽtina confirms the unexpected-onset sense and retains its nasal abbreviation.

runs.text: Hum certo bicho como biſouro que

lines.note: Tonbǒ names the dragonfly, described here by comparison with a beetle-like insect. The gloss and its continuation are preserved rather than replaced by a modern zoological definition.
The insect flies in summer. This seasonal detail completes the preceding Tonbǒ description.
Tonbǒmuſubi is a loop or tying of cords. The following line explains the resemblance to the insect’s wings.

runs.text: à maneira de aſas deste biſouro.

lines.note: The cord arrangement resembles the wings of that insect. The repeated biſouro refers back to the source’s comparison for Tonbǒ and is not a separate species claim.
Tone is an innkeeper who accommodates and assists river travellers. The scan supports nego-, beginning negocea, rather than OCR neço-.

runs.text: cea os que nauegão estes dous rios, Yodo, &

lines.note: Negocea completes the description of serving those navigating the two named rivers. The clear initial Y corrects OCR Podo; Yodo occurs inside the Portuguese explanation.
Cauaxiri completes the pair of river names. Yodo, cauaxirino tone is then the Japanese example for the person associated with those waterways; Eſ- begins the Portuguese restatement.

runs.text: te homem que tem eſte officio como Toi.

lines.note: Completes Este homem: the man performing this office, compared with a Toi. Toi is a Japanese occupational term embedded in the Portuguese explanation.
Tǒnen is glossed by ataru toxi and Este anno: the present year. Retain the printed headword mark and unaccented anno.

runs.text: Homem que tem cuidado dos caualos

lines.note: Toneri is the man responsible for horses, an attendant or groom. The Portuguese comparison with faraz continues below.
Como faraz supplies the comparison for the horse attendant. The unfamiliar occupational word is printed as faraz and is not silently substituted with a modern Portuguese job title.
Tonerico is identified only as the name of a tree. The brief source gloss does not supply a botanical species to add to the transcription.
Tongiacu is explained by musabori tsuku, greedy attachment, and the Portuguese begins with delight or pleasure. The gloss develops its attached state on the next row.
Affection or attachment to something completes the general definition. Togani tongia- starts an example of being attached to wrongdoing.
Cu completes tongiacu, and shite iru expresses remaining in that condition. The Portuguese says immersed or mired in something; nos, visibly with o, corrects OCR nus.
Peccados completes the image of being mired in sins, translating toga in the preceding example. The short line is genuine body text.

runs.text: De qual quer maneira que ſeja, ou

lines.note: Tonicacuni means however it may be or by any means. The final n is visible, correcting the OCR Tonicacuri; the Portuguese retains qual quer as two words.
Por todas as vias completes the range of means: in every possible way. This belongs to Tonicacuni rather than the following date expression.
Tǒnichi, explained by ataru fi, denotes the appointed or relevant day. The Portuguese definition continues with an event falling or occurring on that day.

runs.text: cae algũa festa, ou ſe faz algũa couſa. Vt,

lines.note: The day is when a feast falls or an act takes place. Vt introduces the Christmas example in the next line.

runs.text: Dia em que vẽ o Natal.

lines.note: Natalno tǒnichi means the actual day of Christmas; the Portuguese says the day on which Christmas comes. The capital in Dia is severely abraded and now looks L-like; the aligned OCR reading is retained provisionally, supported by the following ia and the definition above, rather than treating lost ink as a secure printed L.

Tonicǒni is equated with Tonicacuni, giving the same manner or means expression. Abrasion crosses the ǒn, but the surviving strokes and the subsequently consulted NINJAL index, record 260d18, support the chosen reading over OCR Tonicoei. The printed ma continues without a supplied hyphen.

runs.text: neira que ſeja, ou por todas as vias.

lines.note: Neira completes maneira, followed by the same any-way or by-all-means gloss. The break preserves the absence of a printed hyphen after ma in the preceding line.
Tonimocacunimo gives another form of the same irrespective-of-manner expression. The source prints it continuously, and its Portuguese definition continues below.
Que seja completes the phrase meaning in whatever manner it may be. The very short row remains a separate physical line.
Tonimo cǒnimo is referred back to the same meaning by Idem. The visible space and caron are retained rather than regularizing the series of variants.

runs.text: Peßoa que he cabeça, & principal ẽ

lines.note: Tônin is the leading or principal person in a group. The gloss’s qualification continues over the next two lines, and its final nasal abbreviation is retained.

runs.text: algum ajuntamento de gente quer ſeja em boa,

lines.note: The person leads an assembly of people, whether the role is taken in a good sense or otherwise. The continuation qualifies the assessment of the leader.
Ou mà parte completes the possible bad or unfavourable sense, contrasted with em boa. This closes the Tônin entry.

Tonjei, alternatively tonxei, is explained by yo wo nogaruru, withdrawing from the world. The Portuguese begins with shaving oneself; the visible terminal division mark in rapar- is restored before ſe on the next row.

runs.text: ſe deixando a caſa, ou mundo.

lines.note: Completes the account of shaving oneself while abandoning one’s household or the world. Tonjei beneath this line is separately positioned catchword furniture and is not repeated body text.
